oil.summary: Crude surged sharply on Tuesday, with WTI settling at $75.64/bbl (+7.35%) and Brent at $79.94/bbl (+7.77%), as a cascade of geopolitical shocks dominated the tape. Iran attacked commercial vessels in the Strait of Hormuz, prompting U.S. retaliatory strikes on Iranian targets and the immediate revocation of Iran's sanctions waiver, leaving an estimated 63 million barrels of crude stranded at sea. Simultaneously, Ukraine struck eight Russian dark-fleet tankers in the Sea of Azov, with U.S. intelligence reportedly guiding separate drone strikes on Russian refineries. Heating oil outperformed dramatically (+10.73%), reflecting acute supply-chain anxiety. The one bearish note came from EIA data showing a surprise 3.0 million-barrel crude inventory build for the week ending July 3, contrasting with the API's earlier draw estimate of 399,000 barrels. The month-on-month losses of 14-16% underscore how sharply the geopolitical risk premium has re-entered the market.
drivers: U.S. revocation of Iran sanctions waiver and mutual military strikes on Strait of Hormuz shipping lanes, threatening crude flow disruption
Ukraine drone campaign targeting eight Russian dark-fleet tankers in the Sea of Azov, adding further supply-side risk
Bearish offset: EIA reported a surprise 3.0 million-barrel U.S. crude inventory build for the week ending July 3

gas.summary: European gas prices bore the brunt of the Hormuz escalation, with TTF jumping 5.81% on the day to €49.28/MWh and extending a sharp 13.43% weekly rally. The sole headline available today directly links the move to LNG tankers making U-turns after fresh hostilities disrupted vessel traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, a critical artery for LNG flows into Europe. Henry Hub was comparatively unmoved, ticking up just 0.28% to $3.274/MMBtu, consistent with the U.S. market's limited direct exposure to Hormuz transit risk. News flow for this sector is thin beyond the Hormuz disruption headline; further commentary would require additional data.
drivers: LNG tankers diverting or turning back amid renewed Strait of Hormuz hostilities, tightening European supply expectations
TTF weekly gain of 13.43% signals sustained European market anxiety over Middle East supply routes
Henry Hub largely insulated, rising only 0.28% given minimal U.S. direct exposure to Hormuz LNG flows

power.summary: The power and carbon complex presented a mixed picture. EU carbon allowances (EUA) slipped 1.45% to $74.88/EUA, giving back a fraction of the prior month's 4.12% gain, even as TTF's surge nominally raises the cost of gas-fired generation and could support carbon demand. Gulf power infrastructure came into focus as Bahrain and Kuwait moved to restore electricity supplies following Iranian retaliatory strikes on both nations. On the structural side, two separate commentaries flagged growing U.S. grid stress driven by AI-sector electricity demand, with one piece questioning whether Trump's nuclear loan program is adequately sized to address the underlying capacity shortfall. News flow is limited for this sector beyond these themes.
drivers: Iranian strikes on Gulf nations disrupted power infrastructure in Kuwait and Bahrain, highlighting direct conflict risk to regional grids
EUA slipped 1.45% despite higher gas prices; disconnect may reflect near-term demand uncertainty offsetting fuel-switching signals
Structural AI-driven power demand growth is intensifying U.S. grid capacity concerns, with nuclear loan program questioned as insufficient
